title: Newton’s First Law of Motion: Inertia
lead: A body at rest stays at rest and a body in motion keeps moving at a constant velocity unless a net external force acts on it. That is Newton’s first law. Friction, and not the motion itself, brings a sliding object to a halt. The property the law describes is inertia, and mass measures it.
objectives: Understand Newton's first law of motion.
summary_html:
• Newton’s first law of motion states that a body at rest remains at rest, or, if in motion, remains in motion at a constant velocity unless acted on by a net external force. This is also known as the law of inertia.
  • Inertia is the tendency of an object to remain at rest or remain in motion. Inertia is related to an object’s mass.
  • Mass is the quantity of matter in a substance.

exercises.prompt: Which has more mass: a kilogram of cotton balls or a kilogram of gold?

answer.solution: They are equal. A kilogram of one substance is equal in mass to a kilogram of another substance. The quantities that might differ between them are volume and density.

exercises.prompt: How are inertia and mass related?

answer.solution: Inertia is the property of a body that keeps it at rest or keeps it moving at a constant velocity, and mass measures that property. A body with more mass has more inertia, which is why it is harder to change the motion of a large boulder than that of a basketball. You measure mass in kilograms by comparison with the standard kilogram, so measuring a body’s mass puts its inertia into numbers. That is also why people often call Newton’s first law the law of inertia.

exercises.prompt: What is the relationship between weight and mass? Which is an intrinsic, unchanging property of a body?

answer.solution: Mass is the quantity of matter in a body, and weight is the gravitational force that acts on that matter. The two are closely related, but they are not the same quantity and they do not share units. Mass is the intrinsic, unchanging property: an object has the same mass on Earth, in orbit, or on the surface of the Moon, since carrying it somewhere else does not change the number of atoms and molecules in it. Weight changes from place to place, because it depends on the strength of the gravitational pull where the body is.
